## Before we start {.unnumbered}

Make sure your folder structure looks like this and that you have downloaded the required files from OPAL before the session:

```         
intro_to_gis/
├── exercises_code/
│   └── ex_2.qmd       <- this file goes here
└── data/
    └── raw/
        ├── tram_lines.csv        <- from Session 1
        ├── markets.csv           <- from Session 1
        └── gadm41_DEU_shp/       <- NEW: download from OPAL
            ├── gadm41_DEU_0.shp
            ├── gadm41_DEU_1.shp
            ├── gadm41_DEU_2.shp
            ├── gadm41_DEU_3.shp
            ├── gadm41_DEU_4.shp
            └── ... (keep all .prj .dbf .cpg .shx files alongside each .shp)
```

::: callout-tip
## Alternative: download GADM without uploading files

You can also load administrative boundaries directly in R without downloading anything using the `geodata` package. This is shown at the end of the admin boundaries section and is useful for your own projects.
:::

```{r setup}
library(pacman)

pacman::p_load(
  ggplot2,
  dplyr,
  sf,
  rnaturalearth,
  rnaturalearthdata,
  grid,
  ggspatial,
  gridExtra,
  ggrepel,
  tidygeocoder,
  osrm,
  geodata,
  here,
  terra,
  tidyr
)

here::i_am("exercises_code/ex_2.qmd")
```

## Administrative boundaries

One of the most common tasks in applied economics is analysing phenomena across or within administrative units. Survey data are usually geo-located at this level: the dataset contains a municipality code or region name, and to bring this into a spatial framework you need to merge it with a shapefile of the corresponding administrative boundaries.

### The GADM hierarchy

The [GADM database](https://gadm.org/download_country.html) provides boundaries for all countries at multiple administrative levels. The naming convention is:

| Level   | Typical meaning        | NUTS equivalent |
|---------|------------------------|-----------------|
| Admin 0 | Country                | --              |
| Admin 1 | States / Länder        | NUTS 1          |
| Admin 2 | Regions / Kreise       | NUTS 2          |
| Admin 3 | Districts / Landkreise | NUTS 3          |
| Admin 4 | Municipalities         | --              |

Definitions vary by country and can change over time. Always check the `NAME_*` columns to understand what each level represents for the country you are working with.

::: callout-warning
## Shapefiles come in sets of files

When opening a `.shp` file, the `.prj`, `.dbf`, `.cpg`, and `.shx` files with the same name must be in the same folder. If any of them is missing, `st_read()` will fail or return empty geometries.
:::

### Loading and plotting each level

```{r admin-levels}
deu_0 <- st_read(here("data", "raw", "gadm41_DEU_shp", "gadm41_DEU_0.shp"))
deu_1 <- st_read(here("data", "raw", "gadm41_DEU_shp", "gadm41_DEU_1.shp"))
deu_2 <- st_read(here("data", "raw", "gadm41_DEU_shp", "gadm41_DEU_2.shp"))
deu_3 <- st_read(here("data", "raw", "gadm41_DEU_shp", "gadm41_DEU_3.shp"))
deu_4 <- st_read(here("data", "raw", "gadm41_DEU_shp", "gadm41_DEU_4.shp"))

# Check CRS -- should all be WGS84
st_crs(deu_1)$epsg

# Quick plots for each level
ggplot() + geom_sf(data = deu_0) + labs(title = "Admin 0 -- Germany") + theme_minimal()
ggplot() + geom_sf(data = deu_1) + labs(title = "Admin 1 -- Länder") + theme_minimal()
ggplot() + geom_sf(data = deu_2) + labs(title = "Admin 2 -- Kreise") + theme_minimal()
ggplot() + geom_sf(data = deu_4) + labs(title = "Admin 4 -- Municipalities") + theme_minimal()
```

### Filtering to an area of interest

Because sf objects behave like data frames, you can filter them with `dplyr::filter()` using the `NAME_*` columns.

```{r filter-areas}
# List available level-1 names
table(deu_1$NAME_1)

# Keep only Saxony
saxony <- deu_1 |> filter(NAME_1 == "Sachsen")
ggplot() + geom_sf(data = saxony) + labs(title = "Saxony") + theme_minimal()

# Keep only Dresden at the municipality level
dresden <- deu_4 |> filter(NAME_4 == "Dresden")
ggplot() + geom_sf(data = dresden) + labs(title = "Dresden") + theme_minimal()

# Combine levels: all of Saxony at admin-4 detail, with Dresden highlighted
saxony_4 <- deu_4 |> filter(NAME_1 == "Sachsen")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = saxony_4, colour = "darkgreen", fill = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = dresden, aes(fill = "Dresden"), colour = NA) +
  labs(title = "Saxony at municipality level", fill = "") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Alternative: loading GADM directly in R

```{r geodata-gadm}
# geodata::gadm() downloads directly and returns a SpatVector
# Use st_as_sf() to convert to sf for use with ggplot and dplyr
deu_1_online <- geodata::gadm(country = "DEU", level = 1, path = tempdir()) |>
  st_as_sf()

# Identical result, no manual download needed
ggplot() + geom_sf(data = deu_1_online) + theme_minimal()
```

::: callout-note
## Which approach to use?

`geodata::gadm()` is better for reproducibility since anyone can run your code. The manual download is fine for coursework. For your thesis, prefer the programmatic approach and document the download date in a comment.
:::

## Cropping to an area of interest

Sometimes you want to restrict spatial data to an area defined by another spatial object rather than by an administrative name. The `terra::crop()` function cuts a spatial object to the extent of a second object.

```{r crop}
tram_lines <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "tram_lines.csv"), sep = ";")
tram_sf    <- st_as_sf(tram_lines, wkt = "geom")

# Convert to SpatVectors for terra operations
tram_terra    <- vect(tram_sf)
dresden_terra <- vect(dresden)

# Crop Dresden boundaries to the extent of the tram network
area_tram       <- crop(dresden_terra, tram_terra)
area_tram_sf    <- st_as_sf(area_tram)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = dresden) +
  geom_sf(data = area_tram_sf, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4, colour = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Dresden: area covered by trams") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r add-markets}
market    <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "markets.csv"), sep = ";")
market_sf <- st_as_sf(market, wkt = "geom")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = dresden, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_sf(data = area_tram_sf, colour = "steelblue", fill = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = market_sf, colour = "firebrick", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Dresden: tram area and markets") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Distances

### Straight-line distance with `st_distance()`

We will compute the distance from the Hülße-Bau building to each market. First we geocode the address using `tidygeocoder`, which queries OpenStreetMaps to return latitude and longitude.

```{r geocode}
husse_bau <- tibble::tribble(
  ~name, ~addr,
  "Hülße-Bau der TU Dresden", "Helmholtzstraße 10, 01069 Dresden"
)

hub_geocode <- husse_bau |>
  geocode(addr, method = "osm", lat = latitude, long = longitude)

print(hub_geocode)

# Convert to sf object
hub_sf <- st_as_sf(hub_geocode, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
```

```{r sanity-plot}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = dresden, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_sf(data = area_tram_sf, colour = "steelblue", fill = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = market_sf, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_sf(data = hub_sf, colour = "gold", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Hülße-Bau (yellow) and Dresden markets (red)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r distances}
# Reproject to a metric CRS for accurate distance calculation
hub_rp    <- st_transform(hub_sf, crs = 3398)
market_rp <- st_transform(market_sf, crs = 3398)

# st_distance returns a matrix (1 origin x N destinations)
dist_matrix <- st_distance(hub_rp, market_rp)

# Transpose and attach market names
dist_df <- as.data.frame(t(dist_matrix))
names(dist_df) <- "distance_m"
dist_df$strasse <- market_rp$strasse

dist_df |>
  arrange(distance_m) |>
  head(10)
```

::: callout-note
## Projected vs geographic CRS for distances

`st_distance()` works on both geographic (degrees) and projected (metres) CRS, but results differ. For distances within a city, always reproject to a local metric CRS first -- EPSG:3398 works well for Germany.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## OpenStreetMaps routing with `osrm`

`st_distance()` gives straight-line distance. For real travel distances and times, we can use the OpenStreetMaps routing engine through the `osrm` package.

Key functions:

-   `osrmTable()` -- distance or time matrix between many origins and destinations
-   `osrmRoute()` -- the actual shortest path between two points as a LINESTRING
-   `osrmTrip()` -- optimal tour visiting a set of locations

### Travel time between markets

```{r osrm-table}
market_hub_sf <- st_as_sf(
  left_join(dist_df, market_sf, by = "strasse")
)

travel_time <- osrmTable(loc = market_hub_sf)

diag(travel_time$durations) <- NA
cat("Median travel time between any two markets:", median(travel_time$durations, na.rm = TRUE), "minutes\n")
```

### Shortest route from the office to a market

```{r osrm-route}
alaun_platz <- market_sf |> filter(strasse == "Alaunplatz")

route <- osrmRoute(src = hub_sf, dst = alaun_platz)

str(route)  # LINESTRING

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = area_tram_sf, colour = "steelblue", fill = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = market_sf, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_sf(data = hub_sf, colour = "gold", size = 3) +
  geom_sf(data = route, colour = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Shortest route: Hülße-Bau to Alaunplatz") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Zooming in with buffer and centroid

```{r centroid-buffer}
center          <- st_centroid(area_tram_sf)
buffered_area   <- st_buffer(center, dist = 8000)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = buffered_area, colour = "darkgreen", fill = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = tram_sf, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = market_sf, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_sf(data = hub_sf, colour = "gold", size = 3) +
  geom_sf(data = route, colour = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Zoomed view: 8km buffer around tram area center") +
  theme_minimal()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Spatial joins and intersections

We now find which tram line overlaps with the computed route using `st_intersection()`.

```{r spatial-join}
intersection <- st_intersection(route, tram_sf)

table(intersection$strasse)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = buffered_area, colour = "grey80", fill = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = tram_sf, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = route, colour = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_sf(data = intersection, colour = "orchid", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Route / tram line intersection (pink points)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: callout-note
## st_intersects vs st_intersection

`st_intersects()` returns a logical: do these two geometries overlap? `st_intersection()` returns the actual geometry of the overlap. Use the former for filtering, the latter when you need the overlapping shape itself.
:::

## Exercise 1 -- Admin boundaries

Using `deu_2` (Kreise level):

1.  Filter to keep only the Kreise belonging to Saxony (`NAME_1 == "Sachsen"`).
2.  Plot them coloured by `NAME_2`.
3.  Compute the centroid of each Kreis using `st_centroid()` and add them as points on the same map.
4.  How many Kreise does Saxony have? Use `nrow()`.
:::

::: callout-caution
## Exercise 2 -- Distance from your location

Pick any address in Dresden that is meaningful to you (where you live, your favourite café, etc.).

1.  Geocode it using `tidygeocoder`.
2.  Compute the straight-line distance to all markets.
3.  Find the nearest market and compute the `osrmRoute()` to it.
4.  Plot the route on top of the tram network.
:::
